display: Frederick Law Olmsted was born in Hartford, Connecticut, on April 26, 1822.
Olmsted died on August 28, 1903, in Belmont, Massachusetts, at 81.
Olmsted ceased active practice in 1895, a victim of failing memory and vitality; later accounts say dementia, or senility, forced his retirement, and his sons took over the firm.

His health continued to fail after he retired. A trip to England did not help, and he became depressed there; a summer house built on Deer Isle, Maine, in 1897 was laid out to stimulate his decreasing mental abilities, but after one summer there his health continued to deteriorate.
Olmsted, who had chosen the Belmont site of McLean Hospital in 1872, was admitted there as a patient at the end of his life and spent his last five years there, until his death in 1903.
His McLean Hospital medical record is sealed, and the cause of his decline is not known.
Any specific type of dementia (for example Alzheimer's disease or vascular dementia) is a retrospective interpretation; the cited sources say only failing memory, senility, and dementia.

A psychiatrist has argued retrospectively that losses in his childhood, beginning with his mother's death when he was a young child, left him with post-traumatic stress, and that his late illness made it worse.
In 1863, exhausted and ill after overwork as head of the U.S. Sanitary Commission, Olmsted resigned.
